title: It grows
hookLine: a study tested whether weeks of loving-kindness practice change a person's days

lines: A TEAM DECIDED TO FIND OUT.
cards: May all beings be happy. That's the heart of an old Buddhist teaching, the Metta Sutta, which describes a love meant to reach every living thing, near and far, seen and unseen.
Say a sentence like that, and a fair question comes up. Does saying it change anything in the one who says it? A team of psychologists decided to find out.
They taught a group of working adults a loving-kindness meditation, then followed them week after week, asking each evening how the day had gone inside.

teach.b: First, a practice, not a mood. The Metta Sutta speaks of cultivating a boundless heart toward all beings, the way a mother guards her only child.
Buddhist teachers call metta a practice: you bring someone to mind and wish them well on purpose, whether or not the warmth shows up.
Second, the study. Psychologist Barbara Fredrickson and her colleagues ran it. Some participants learned loving-kindness meditation; a comparison group waited their turn for the course.
Both kept reporting on their days. Over the weeks, the meditators reported more positive emotions in ordinary life: joy, gratitude, contentment, hope and love.
Third, small days, stacked up. The gains didn't arrive on day one. The paper describes them showing up gradually, as people kept practicing.
Nobody flipped a switch. Something got watered.
Fourth, what it built. Fredrickson's larger idea is called broaden and build: good feelings widen what a person notices, and over time they build lasting resources.
The meditators also reported more sense of purpose, more support from others, and more satisfaction with their lives. Now the honest part.
This is one study. People reported on themselves, and the changes were modest. It proves nothing about the deep nature of love.
But on one plain point it agrees with the old sutta: this kind of love is something a person can grow.

how: Buddhist meditators practice loving-kindness (metta) by silently wishing well to themselves and others in widening circles, often for a set time each day; the practice is also taught in secular meditation courses and has been studied by psychologists.

games.q: you've just started a loving-kindness course. week one, and it feels like nothing. what do you do?
o: quit: it clearly doesn't work for you.

games.why: in the study the gains came gradually, over weeks of practice. that's the title: it grows.

practice: Bring to mind someone easy to love, a friend, a grandparent, a pet, and silently offer them the kind of wish the practice uses: may you be well, may you be at ease.
Stay with this one person, repeating the wish at the pace of the breath; if warmth comes, fine, and if it doesn't, keep going anyway, the way a gardener waters the same bed every day.
If you pray, you can hold them before God as you go.

wordCard.voice: It grows. Loving-kindness treated as a practice that strengthens with use, as the Metta Sutta teaches and a modern study set out to test. Today's word.

orig.note: metta, the Pali word for loving-kindness, from the Buddhist tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: something got watered. Love like this is grown, a little at a time. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.
